TITLE: Evaluating LLMs' Learning Capacity on Mathematical Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment where LLMs are trained on a sequence of progressively harder mathematical reasoning problems (e.g., SAT, GRE Quant, calculus, and proveability of famous math theorems), and their performance is evaluated after each problem. We test popular LLMs (e.g., RoBERTa and BART) on three different training regimens: incremental learning, where a model is fine-tuned on each subsequent problem without forgetting previous knowledge; transfer learning, where a single model is pre-trained on all problems at once; and no prior knowledge, where each model learns a problem from scratch.
CONTROLS: Three ablations serve as controls: (1) same LLM trained on a single task, (2) the same number of LLMs trained on multiple tasks without cumulative knowledge, and (3) identical tasks with preorder difficulty adjustment trained on the same sets of models for between about 5- 10 iterations with fewer number of samples for each.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect models trained with incremental learning to exhibit significant improvements across tasks as they gain experience, and that transfer learning will significantly outperform incremental learning due to its ability to leverage prior experience across multiple tasks, while models learning from scratch will struggle to learn successfully as they don't have information from the previous examples to relate and improve their attention to relevant information.

Specifically, we will add a series of transfer tasks that test the model's ability to generalize to new mathematical reasoning problems, with increasing complexity and abstractness. We will also investigate the effect of different pre-training objectives on the model's ability to generalize to these transfer tasks.
CONTROLS: We maintain our previous controls, which include three ablations: (1) same LLM trained on a single task, (2) the same number of LLMs trained on multiple tasks without cumulative knowledge, and (3) identical tasks with preorder difficulty adjustment trained on the same sets of models for between about 5- 10 iterations with fewer number of samples for each.
COST: 900 GPU-hours

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating LLMs' Ability to Learn and Adapt in Text Classification and Summarization
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether LLMs can learn and adapt to new text classification and summarization tasks by drawing on prior experience with similar tasks. We design an experiment where LLMs are trained on a sequence of text classification and summarization tasks with increasing difficulty, and their performance is evaluated after each task. We also investigate the effect of different learning rates and optimization strategies on the model's ability to adapt to new tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) benchmark LLMs trained on a single task, (2) the same number of LLMs trained on multiple tasks without cumulative knowledge, (3) identical tasks with adjusted difficulty trained on the same sets of models.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the LLMs to exhibit improved accuracy and adaptation speed as they progress through the sequence of tasks, particularly when using optimized learning rates and optimization strategies. However, we also anticipate that the models may suffer from overfitting and loss of generalization ability if the adaptation process is too aggressive or if the tasks become too dissimilar.

Additionally, we plan to investigate the relationship between the model's ability to learn and adapt and its capacity to generalize to new tasks. Specifically, we will explore the hypothesis that the capacity for generalization is crucial for learning and adaptation, while the ability to learn and adapt is necessary but not sufficient for generalization.

TITLE: Evaluating LLMs' Ability to Learn and Adapt in Text Classification and Summarization
PROPOSAL: Update the design of our fifth experiment to focus specifically on the text summarization task, and to use a more nuanced evaluation metric that captures both the accuracy and coherence of the generated summaries. We will also investigate the effect of different summarization objectives, such as extractive and abstractive summarization, on the model's ability to adapt to new tasks.
CONTROLS: We maintain our previous controls, which include (1) benchmark LLMs trained on a single task, (2) the same number of LLMs trained on multiple tasks without cumulative knowledge, and (3) identical tasks with adjusted difficulty trained on the same sets of models. Additionally, we will test the models on real-world text summarization datasets, such as the CNN/Daily Mail and the New York Times Annotated Corpus datasets.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the LLMs to exhibit improved summarization quality and coherence as they progress through the sequence of tasks, particularly when using optimally tuned summarization objectives. However, we also anticipate that the models may suffer from overfitting or underfitting if the summarization objectives or evaluation metrics are inadequate for the task at hand.

Note: This revised experiment focuses more precisely on text summarization, addresses a more specific aspect of the learning and adaptation process, and includes a more targeted evaluation approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Multimodal Feedback in LLMs' Learning and Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to investigate whether LLMs benefit from multimodal feedback (e.g., text, images, and audio) when learning and adapting to new tasks. We will train LLMs using multimodal feedback datasets, such as the Visual Genome and the ALGAN datasets, and compare their performance to LLMs trained using unimodal feedback datasets.
CONTROLS: (1) benchmark LLMs trained on unimodal feedback datasets, (2) the same number of LLMs trained on multimodal feedback datasets without cumulative knowledge, (3) identical tasks with adjusted difficulty trained on the same sets of models.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the LLMs to exhibit improved learning and adaptation performance when trained using multimodal feedback datasets, particularly for tasks that require understanding and integrating multiple types of information. However, we also anticipate that the benefit of multimodal feedback may be task-dependent and that the models may not always benefit from it, especially for tasks that require specialized or domain-specific knowledge.

This experiment will provide insights into the importance of multimodal feedback in LLMs' learning and adaptation processes and will inform the design of more effective multimodal feedback mechanisms for future LLMs.
